name: Ethics Review with AI Assistance
title: Ethics Review with AI Assistance
answer: Ethics review with AI assistance covers the use of machine learning tools inside institutional review boards, research ethics committees, and similar bodies that assess human subjects research, animal work, and dual use concerns. It spans the drafting of consent forms, the screening of protocols for missing safeguards, the triage of submissions by risk level, and the summarising of prior decisions so that reviewers can compare a new study against precedent. The scope is procedural rather than substantive: the tool supports the committee's judgement, it does not replace the committee's authority to approve, conditionally approve, or reject a study.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Ethics review with AI assistance covers the use of machine learning tools inside institutional review boards, research ethics committees, and similar bodies that assess human subjects research, animal work, and dual use concerns. It spans the drafting of consent forms, the screening of protocols for missing safeguards, the triage of submissions by risk level, and the summarising of prior decisions so that reviewers can compare a new study against precedent. The scope is procedural rather than substantive: the tool supports the committee's judgement, it does not replace the committee's authority to approve, conditionally approve, or reject a study.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run on document processing pipelines that ingest protocols, consent forms, and investigator responses in common formats such as PDF and DOCX. Retrieval layers index an institution's own policy library and past minutes so that a reviewer's question can be matched against the wording that governed earlier cases. Language models handle summarisation and question answering, while rule engines or classifiers flag specific items like vulnerable populations, payment amounts, or data sharing clauses. Access is usually confined to a secure institutional environment because the material contains unpublished research and personal data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a structured intake step that splits a submission into sections and extracts the claims a reviewer needs to check. A screening pass then compares those claims against a checklist drawn from the institution's policies and the relevant regulatory framework, producing a list of items that appear addressed, missing, or ambiguous. Reviewers read the flagged items alongside the original text, and any tool output is treated as a prompt for human attention rather than a finding. Records of what the tool surfaced and what the reviewer concluded are kept together so the reasoning behind a decision remains traceable.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Accountability stays with the named reviewers and the committee chair, and the tool's role is documented in the meeting record. Institutions need a clear position on what may be sent to an external model provider, how long inputs are retained, and whether submissions can be used to improve a vendor's system. Bias in screening matters because a classifier trained on past approvals can reproduce earlier patterns of over or under scrutiny against particular fields, institutions, or populations. Provenance of any cited policy or precedent should point to the original document rather than a paraphrase, so that a reviewer can verify the source directly.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Near term development is likely to focus on better integration with submission systems, so that screening happens at intake rather than as a separate step. Expect more attention to evaluation, with institutions asking for evidence that a tool catches the same problems a human reviewer would catch and does not generate false alarms that slow the queue. Shared benchmarks and reporting standards for ethics review tools would make comparison between systems possible. The harder question is whether assisted review changes the substance of decisions over time, and that will only be answered by tracking outcomes across many committees.
